description: We’re a team of engineering students from UCD with backgrounds in robotics, electronics and hackathons, tackling the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. Our team is already complete, so we’re not looking for new members, but good luck to everyone taking part!
summary:
Beacon is a live survival-routing system for astronauts on a Marswalk. Our terrain engine reads real 1 m HiRISE terrain and computes, for every point, radiation exposure, sunlight, and line of sight to base and Earth. It plans walks with science stops, finds natural shelters, and re-plans live as conditions change: rerouting to the lowest-dose cover when a solar storm hits, and using heart rate, exertion, oxygen and water to call the astronaut back before supplies run short. It runs across three linked devices: a command hub in the habitat, a heads-up display built into the helmet visor, and a suit-mounted wrist unit with a map, glove-friendly emergency controls and an alarm.

The challenge asks for a hyperlocal, multi-mission map an astronaut can walk with. Beacon layers HiRISE, MOLA, Curiosity RAD, REMS, DONKI and JPL Horizons data at two real sites, Gale and Jezero craters. Our radiation model came within 3% of Curiosity’s measurement at Murray Buttes and is driven by the real May 2024 storm.

It matters because Earth is up to 22 light-minutes away, and on 20 May 2024 Curiosity recorded radiation 56 times normal. On Mars, safety decisions can’t wait.
details:
What it does
Beacon is a live survival-routing system for astronauts on a Marswalk. It reads real Mars terrain metre by metre and continuously plans the safest route based on both the environment and the astronaut. When conditions change, from a solar storm to rising exertion or falling supplies, it re-plans the walk and tells the astronaut where to go.

How it works

  1. Skyline engine. For every point, Beacon traces the terrain horizon in 360 directions. It uses 1 m HiRISE terrain out to 700 m, then coarser terrain and MOLA out to 300 km, including planetary curvature. The fraction of sky the terrain blocks gives radiation shielding. Comparing the skyline with JPL Horizons Sun and Earth positions gives sunlight and direct-to-Earth visibility. A base radio mast gives the comms link.
  2. Shelters and routes. Natural shelters are found automatically: spots with far more blocked sky than open ground, gentle slopes and room to wait. That gives 35 at Murray Buttes in Gale crater and 19 at Jezero crater. Routes follow the real terrain, slow down on slopes, avoid ground steeper than 25°, and include science stops.
  3. Radiation dose. The dose model combines three measured inputs:
    • Curiosity’s measured quiet dose rate (6.3 µGy/h).
    • The real 20 May 2024 solar storm (33× normal over the first four hours).
    • A terrain-shielding factor calibrated to Curiosity’s measurement at Murray Butte (Ehresmann et al. 2021).
  4. Storm decision. When a storm is declared, the astronaut must be under cover before it arrives. Among the places reachable in time, Beacon picks the one with the lowest total dose, and the shielded base wins whenever it is in reach. If nothing can be reached in time, the reroute is flagged late rather than hidden.
  5. Astronaut-aware routing. Wrist sensors report heart rate, SpO2 and skin temperature. From these Beacon estimates exertion and how fast oxygen, cooling water, drinking water and suit power are being used. It keeps a live safety margin: the scarcest supply left, minus the walking time back to safety. As exertion rises or supplies fall, it trims or reorders science stops, avoids steep, tiring ground, and calls “turn back now” before the margin runs out. Crew condition and past-walk heart rates shape each plan before the walk.
  6. Linked devices. Everything runs across three linked devices:
    One shared mission state keeps them in sync, so a storm declared at the hub instantly reroutes the visor and wrist.
    • A command hub in the habitat for planning and storm control.
    • A heads-up display in the helmet visor.
    • A suit-mounted wrist unit with a map, glove-friendly emergency controls and an alarm.

Validation
In 2016 Curiosity parked beside Murray Butte and measured that the terrain blocked about 19% of the sky. Working from terrain alone, and never given that number, Beacon’s engine came within 3% of Curiosity’s measured value.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Safety decisions in seconds, when Earth can be up to 22 light-minutes away.
  • The lowest radiation dose reasonably achievable on every walk, which protects astronauts’ career radiation limits.
  • Safer, longer, more productive science excursions, with supplies and exertion managed live.
  • One engine for any site with terrain data, from other Mars sites to the lunar south pole for Artemis.
  • On Earth, the same approach can also be applied to mountain rescue, flood response and professionals combating wildfires.

How it is creative
Existing tools either map the whole planet (like JPL Mars Trek) or rely on routes planned on Earth before the walk. Beacon turns terrain into safety: one skyline calculation gives radiation, sunlight and comms at metre scale. It combines this with the astronaut’s own body and supplies to make live decisions. Those decisions reach the astronaut on their visor and wrist, not just on a screen at base.

Factors we considered

  • Communication delay: decisions must be made locally, not on Earth.
  • Forecast uncertainty: storm forecasts set the go/no-go days ahead; live rerouting handles what forecasts miss.
  • Suited mobility: walking speed, slope limits and glove-friendly hold-to-confirm controls, so a bump can’t trigger an alarm.
  • Redundancy: the wrist works if the visor fails, with sound, light and touch alerts.
  • Honesty about limits: doses are absorbed dose, not health risk; the model covers terrain shielding only, not suit shielding; it uses one storm profile; shelters need checking on the ground.

What we built this weekend
In 48 hours we built a fully working, connected prototype:

  • A Meta Quest 3 visor app in AR and VR, overlaying the live mission and walking real HiRISE-based Mars terrain.
  • An ESP32-S3 wrist cuff with guarded SOS, reroute and acknowledge buttons, LEDs, a siren and a gyro wrist-flick to acknowledge alarms, alongside a phone wrist map.
  • A command hub dashboard with a Mars globe, terrain layers, route planner, crew status with a live safety margin, and storm controls.
  • A Rust engine doing every calculation from real NASA data.

Fully automatic re-planning from exertion and supplies is the next step.

Tools, languages and hardware

  • Languages and frameworks: Rust (terrain engine), Node.js (relay), JavaScript with three.js and Vite (hub and wrist), C# with Unity/OpenXR (Meta Quest 3), Python with GDAL and Rasterio (data preparation), C++ with Arduino/PlatformIO (firmware).
  • Hardware: ESP32-S3, MPU-9250 motion sensor, MAX30102 heart-rate sensor, buttons, LEDs and buzzer on perfboard, in a 3D-printed forearm mount designed in Onshape.
